extracted.intended_audience: Regulated entities, facility operators, environmental consultants, State regulators, and stakeholders commenting on EPA CCR rulemaking
extracted.subtask_short: assessing risks from legacy CCR units
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and justification for how EPA evaluates human health and groundwater risks from legacy coal combustion residual (CCR) surface impoundments, landfills, and smaller CCR management unit (CCRMU) placements when developing national regulatory requirements. Focuses on modeling choices, scenarios (including future land use), data sources, and limitations of national-scale risk assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the 2014 Risk Assessment to legacy and inactive units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's determination that the 2014 Risk Assessment results are equally applicable to legacy CCR surface impoundments and CCRMU because many unregulated units are similarly constructed, manage the same types of ash, and are frequently collocated with regulated units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains the 2014 Risk Assessment modeled the unit lifecycle stage anticipated to contribute most to long-term risk (surface impoundments during operation; landfills after closure) and tracked subsequent groundwater migration. Existing groundwater contamination does not vanish when a unit ceases operation. EPA cites state program variability, monitoring reports showing corrective actions, and photographic evidence (e.g., vegetation compromising caps) as support for applying the 2014 results to historical and inactive units. The response also notes excluded units previously modeled with similar sizes and conditions, so national results remain representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select lifecycle stage that contributes most to long-term risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the specific lifecycle stage of a disposal unit that is anticipated to contribute the most to long-term offsite risk (e.g., operation stage for surface impoundments; post-closure for landfills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA states selection of a single lifecycle stage was necessary because of model constraints and computational burden. The assessment modeled leakage occurring over that stage and tracked migration through groundwater over time as representative of long-term risk. This approach is appropriate even if unit configuration changes later (e.g., capped or drained) because contamination that occurred during the high-risk stage can persist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a probabilistic, site-based national modeling approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine site-specific data with regional and national data sources to produce a probabilistic, site-based model that characterizes national-scale risk distributions rather than exact risk at each individual site.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA incorporated data on location, dimensions, and liner status where available. The model's aim is to provide an overall accurate picture of potential risks at the national scale. Damage cases supplement the model where site conditions could not be modeled. EPA acknowledges that some individual site conditions (e.g., waste below the water table) could not be adequately modeled and thus national estimates may understate some high-end risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Reasonable Maximum Exposure (RME) as the principal evaluation basis
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate potential human health risks based on an RME scenario — a conservative, high-end exposure scenario intended to protect sensitive populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA defines the RME/high-end as the part of the exposure distribution above the 90th percentile but below the 99.9th percentile. The RME is intended to remain within the range of possible high-end exposures while protecting sensitive populations. Critiques that the risk assessment is overly conservative are addressed by noting the RME remains a standard practice under RCRA and other programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of future residential land use and local population radii
rubrics_metrics.description: Include future onsite residential exposure scenarios and population estimates within specified radii (one-, three-, and five-mile) when evaluating risks and the potential for redevelopment of facility lands to residential uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA argues five miles is a reasonable distance for potential residential expansion and that evidence exists of facility lands being redeveloped for residential use (22 examples noted). The 2024 Risk Assessment updated population estimates to align more closely with the RIA and to include multiple radii. EPA also emphasizes that residential is not the only scenario considered and that non-residential uses (recreation, preserves) can also present exposure pathways if ash is disturbed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baseline risk assessment assumption of no institutional controls (no action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct a baseline risk analysis assuming no actions to control or mitigate releases (i.e., absence of institutional controls) to characterize potential adverse health effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains the baseline (no-action) analysis is used to determine the scope of national minimum criteria and to understand harms that could occur without deed restrictions or other controls. This supports establishing national requirements (for example, deed restrictions for CCRMU that remain in place). EPA notes that due diligence and existing State requirements cannot be assumed to reliably identify all CCRMU placements because records are often incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliance on damage cases to identify additional constituents of potential concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Use documented damage cases to supplement modeling and identify additional constituents of potential concern for groundwater monitoring when certain site conditions could not be modeled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA acknowledges model constraints (e.g., inability to model waste below the water table) and thus relies on damage cases to help identify constituents and scenarios that the models may not capture, ensuring monitoring focuses on constituents demonstrated to cause harm in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modeling smaller CCRMU placements and fillings
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly model placement of CCR in smaller quantities (smaller CCRMU fills) to determine potential for these smaller placements to contaminate groundwater and contribute to facility-scale contamination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA conducted model runs for smaller CCRMU placements showing potential exceedance of groundwater protection standards at the fill boundary, substantial plume spread, and persistence (under high-end conditions plumes can sustain exposures for over a century at average risks ≥ 2×10^-5). EPA also notes that concentrations from individual CCRMU can combine with other on-site sources to increase the likelihood of off-site contaminant plumes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of radiation exposure pathways from CCR
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate potential for radiation exposure (radon and gamma radiation) from CCR remaining in subsurface or mixed with surface soil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA found radon emissions from CCR indistinguishable from background and did not retain radon as a primary pathway. However, gamma radiation risk increases as CCR is located closer to the ground surface. A sensitivity analysis indicated that an eight percent mixture of CCR in surface soil at high-end waste concentrations could produce risk on the order of 1×10^-4. EPA also notes incidental ingestion of arsenic and radium as exposure concerns when CCR mixes with surface soil.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of unit construction and management practices that increase leakage
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for practices more prevalent in legacy units that can increase leakage and risk, such as unlined units, co-management with coal refuse/other wastes (affecting pH), and units constructed below or inundated by the water table.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA proposed that these factors could lead to higher leakage than modeled for active units and estimated lifetime cancer and noncancer risks for certain constituents could be substantially higher (e.g., lifetime cancer risks from arsenic up to 1×10^-3; HQs for cobalt and mercury up to 13). Each practice individually can pose greater risks and combinations could push risks higher. EPA also acknowledges inability to fully model disposal below the water table, meaning some risks are understated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between ponded water and porewater/residual water in impoundments
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between ponded wastewater above ash (which creates large hydraulic head and greater leakage) and porewater/residual water remaining after dewatering (which can still drive leakage but at reduced rates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA clarifies the conceptual model: the highest leakage rates are expected during operation when ponded water exists. Draining reduces hydraulic head but residual water can be substantial (closed impoundments sometimes remain saturated by 20–54 feet of groundwater) and can result in continued leakage similar to landfill dry-management scenarios modeled previously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of monitoring reports and facility-provided data as evidence of risk and management effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate monitoring reports and data from facilities and State program reviews to assess prevalence of corrective actions and variability in oversight and protectiveness among State programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA cites monitoring reports showing approximately 20% of currently active landfills have triggered corrective action and provides percentages for categories of units (e.g., units managing bottom ash or slag showing corrective action rates). EPA also references its 2015 review of State programs (16 States responsible for ~74% of CCR generation in 2009) to demonstrate variability in oversight and that a portion of net disposable CCR was exempt from State oversight in 2015.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit size and aggregation considerations for national risk modeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that individual unit footprint size is not necessarily predictive of overall facility risk; consider that multiple units may be adjacent and their combined leakage can raise site risks beyond single-unit modeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA disagrees that smaller average sizes for legacy units necessarily imply lower national risk, noting the 2014 Risk Assessment modeled units as small as 2 acres (landfills) and 0.01 acres (impoundments). EPA observes many sites with adjacent units where combined leakage over a contributing area could increase risk, and the national model may have underestimated site risk by not evaluating combined leakage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of available data and exclusion of poorly-documented placement types
rubrics_metrics.description: Where specific placement configurations (e.g., roadways, construction fills, storage in waste piles, spreading on roadways) lack sufficient information on frequency or manner of placement, these configurations may be excluded from the conceptual model or considered outside the scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA explains that some placement types are already regulated (waste piles) or lack data sufficient to characterize them nationally, so they are not included in the CCRMU fills conceptual model. Commenters were not shown to demonstrate how these placements would be substantially different from previously modeled disposal scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of third-party reports as supplementary information only
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not rely on third-party investigative reports (e.g., Environmental Integrity Project) as primary basis for rulemaking; use them only as supplementary corroborative information when modeling and damage cases support similar findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA acknowledges methodological differences between such reports and regulatory corrective action standards, and therefore uses such reports as supplementary support for constituents and trends already identified by the 2014 Risk Assessment, rather than as a primary evidentiary basis for the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgment that inability to model certain scenarios understates risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly acknowledge that inability to incorporate some site conditions (notably disposal below the water table) into groundwater fate-and-transport modeling likely causes national risk estimates to underestimate higher leaching/reducing-condition risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA admits both the 2014 and 2024 Risk Assessments did not directly model contact with groundwater because of data and model constraints, and that omission means the assessment underestimates risks associated with higher rates of leaching or formation of strongly reducing conditions. This supports reliance on damage cases and conservative assumptions elsewhere in the assessment.
